title: The Phases of the Moon
summary: Why the Moon seems to change shape during a month: it reflects sunlight, and as it orbits Earth we see different amounts of its lit half.
poll: The Moon really changes its shape during the month.

versions.title: The Moon Changes Shape
versions.text:
Look up at night. Do you see the Moon? Its shape seems to change. But the Moon is the same.

The Moon does not make light. The Sun shines on it. The Moon will reflect that light. That is why it glows.

The Sun lights half of the Moon. It is the half that faces the Sun. The far half is dark.

The Moon goes around Earth. This path is its orbit. One trip takes a month.

As the Moon moves, we see more or less of the lit half. Each shape is a phase.

First we see no Moon at all. Then we see a thin crescent. It grows to half. Then it grows to a full, round Moon. Then it shrinks back.

The dark part is not a shadow from Earth. It is just the side the Sun does not light.

The same side of the Moon faces us all the time.

In Saudi Arabia, each month of the Hijri calendar starts when the new crescent is seen.

You can test this. Shine a lamp on a ball. Walk the ball in a ring. Watch its shape change!

versions.title: The Moon Changes Shape
versions.text:
Look up at the sky at night. Do you see the Moon? Its shape seems to change from night to night. But the Moon does not change at all.

The Moon does not make its own light. The Sun shines on it. The Moon will reflect the light of the Sun. That is why it looks bright.

The Sun always lights half of the Moon. That is the half that faces the Sun. The other half is dark.

The Moon moves in a big ring around Earth. This path is called its orbit. One trip takes about a month.

As the Moon moves, we see more or less of its bright half. Each shape we see is called a phase.

At first, we can not see the Moon at all. Then we see a thin crescent. It grows into a half Moon. Next, it grows into a full, round Moon. Then it shrinks back again.

The dark part is not a shadow from Earth. It is just the side that the Sun does not light.

The same side of the Moon faces us all the time.

In Saudi Arabia, each month of the Hijri calendar starts when people see the new crescent.

You can try this at home. Shine a lamp on a ball. Move the ball in a ring around your head. Watch its shape change!

versions.title: Why the Moon Changes Shape
versions.text:
Look at the sky for a few nights in a row. The Moon seems to change shape. One night it is a thin curve. A week later it is a bright circle. But the Moon itself never changes.

The Moon does not make its own light. Instead, it is lit by the Sun. The Moon's rocky ground can reflect sunlight, so it shines in our night sky.

The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. That is the half that faces the Sun. The other half is in darkness.

The Moon travels in a path around Earth. This path is called its orbit. One full trip takes about a month.

As the Moon moves along its orbit, we see different amounts of its sunny half. Each shape we see is called a phase.

At the start, the sunny side faces away from us, so we can not see the Moon. This is the new Moon. Then a thin crescent appears. It grows into a half Moon and then a full Moon. After that, it shrinks night by night until it is gone again.

Many people think the dark part is Earth's shadow. It is not. It is just the side of the Moon that is facing away from the Sun.

The Moon always shows the same face to Earth.

In Saudi Arabia, each month of the Hijri calendar begins when people see the new crescent.

You can test this with a lamp and a ball. Move the ball in a circle around your head and watch its shape change.

versions.title: Why the Moon Changes Shape
versions.text:
Watch the night sky for a few weeks. You will notice that the Moon seems to change shape. One night it is a thin, curved sliver. About a week later it is a bright circle. Yet the Moon itself never really changes.

The Moon does not make any light of its own. Instead, sunlight falls on it, and its gray, rocky surface can reflect that light back toward Earth.

The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon, the half that faces the Sun. The other half stays dark.

The Moon travels around Earth in a path called its orbit. One complete trip takes about a month, or a little more than 29 days.

As the Moon moves along its orbit, we see different amounts of its sunlit half. Each shape we see is called a phase.

At the beginning, the sunlit side faces away from us, so the Moon is nearly impossible to see. This is the new Moon. Next, a thin crescent appears. It grows into a half Moon, and then into a full Moon. After that, the bright part shrinks night by night until the cycle starts again.

Many people believe the dark part is Earth's shadow, but that is a mistake. It is simply the side of the Moon facing away from the Sun.

The Moon also keeps the same face turned toward Earth all the time.

In Saudi Arabia, each month of the Hijri calendar begins when the new crescent is seen.

To test this, shine a lamp on a ball and move the ball in a circle around your head.

versions.title: The Phases of the Moon
versions.text:
If you look at the night sky for a few weeks, you will see that the Moon seems to change shape. One evening it is a thin, curved sliver. About a week later it has become a bright, round circle. Yet the Moon itself never actually changes.

The Moon does not produce any light of its own. Instead, sunlight falls on its gray, rocky surface, which reflects some of that light toward Earth.

The Sun always lights up exactly half of the Moon, the half that faces the Sun. The other half remains dark.

The Moon travels around Earth in a path called its orbit. It completes one cycle of shapes in about 29 and a half days, which is roughly a month.

As the Moon moves along its orbit, we see different amounts of its illuminated half. Each of these shapes is called a phase.

At the new Moon, the sunlit side faces away from us, so the Moon is almost invisible. Next, a thin crescent appears. The bright part keeps growing, which scientists call waxing, until we see a half Moon and then a full Moon. After that, the bright part shrinks, which is called waning, until the cycle starts again. The phases just before and after the full Moon, when more than half is lit, are called gibbous.

Many people believe that the dark part is Earth's shadow, but this is not true. It is simply the side of the Moon facing away from the Sun.

The Moon also keeps the same side turned toward Earth at all times.

In Saudi Arabia, each month of the Hijri calendar begins when people see the new crescent after sunset.

You can model this with a lamp and a ball.

versions.title: The Phases of the Moon
versions.text:
Anyone who observes the night sky over several consecutive weeks will notice that the Moon appears to transform its shape, shifting from a delicate, curved sliver to a brilliant circle in roughly a week. Nevertheless, the Moon itself never actually changes; only our view of it does.

The Moon generates no light of its own. Instead, sunlight strikes its gray, rocky surface, which reflects a portion of that light back toward Earth, so the lunar glow we admire is really borrowed sunshine.

At every moment, the Sun illuminates exactly one hemisphere of the Moon, namely the half facing the Sun, while the opposite hemisphere remains in complete darkness.

The Moon travels around Earth along a path called its orbit, completing one entire cycle of shapes in approximately 29 and a half days, which corresponds roughly to a calendar month.

As the Moon progresses along its orbit, observers on Earth see varying portions of its illuminated hemisphere, and each of these appearances is called a phase.

At the new Moon, the sunlit hemisphere faces away from us, rendering the Moon practically invisible. Shortly afterward, a slender crescent emerges, and the bright portion continues expanding, a stage astronomers describe as waxing, until a half Moon and eventually a full Moon appear. Subsequently, the bright portion diminishes, which is called waning, until the cycle begins again. The phases immediately before and after the full Moon, when more than half the disk is lit, are described as gibbous.

A widespread misconception holds that the dark portion represents Earth's shadow, but this explanation is incorrect, since it is simply the side of the Moon facing away from the Sun.

Furthermore, because the Moon takes as long to rotate once as it does to orbit Earth, it always keeps the same side turned toward us.

In Saudi Arabia, each month of the Hijri calendar officially begins when the new crescent is sighted after sunset. Because a full cycle lasts about 29 and a half days, every Hijri month has either 29 or 30 days.

You can demonstrate these phases yourself with a lamp and a ball. Darken a room and switch on the lamp. Then hold the ball at arm's length and turn slowly in a circle. As you turn, the lit part of the ball will grow from a crescent to a full circle and then shrink again. In this model, the lamp is the Sun, the ball is the Moon, and your head is Earth.

versions.text:

At every moment, the Sun illuminates precisely one hemisphere of the Moon, namely the half facing the Sun, while the opposite hemisphere remains in complete darkness.

The Moon travels around Earth along a path called its orbit, completing one entire cycle of shapes in approximately 29 and a half days, an interval that corresponds roughly to a calendar month.

As the Moon progresses along its orbit, observers on Earth perceive varying portions of its illuminated hemisphere, and astronomers refer to each of these appearances as a phase.

At the new Moon, the sunlit hemisphere faces away from us, rendering the Moon practically invisible. Shortly afterward, a slender crescent emerges, and the bright portion continues expanding, a stage astronomers describe as waxing, until a half Moon and eventually a full Moon become visible. Subsequently, the bright portion diminishes, which is called waning, until the cycle recommences. A widespread misconception maintains that the dark portion represents Earth's shadow, but this explanation is incorrect, since it is simply the side of the Moon oriented away from the Sun.

In Saudi Arabia, each month of the Hijri calendar officially commences when the new crescent is sighted after sunset, and because a complete cycle lasts approximately 29 and a half days, every Hijri month contains either 29 or 30 days.

You can demonstrate these phases yourself using a lamp and a ball. Darken a room, switch on the lamp, hold the ball at arm's length, and turn slowly in a circle. At every moment, the Sun illuminates precisely one hemisphere of the Moon, namely the half oriented toward the Sun, while the opposite hemisphere remains in complete darkness.

The Moon travels around Earth along a path called its orbit, completing one entire cycle of appearances in approximately 29 and a half days, an interval that corresponds roughly to a calendar month.

versions.title: The Phases of the Moon
versions.text:
Anyone who systematically observes the night sky over several consecutive weeks will notice that the Moon appears to transform its shape, shifting from a delicate, curved sliver to a brilliant, luminous circle in approximately a week. Nevertheless, the Moon itself never genuinely changes; only our geometric perspective on it does.

The Moon generates no illumination whatsoever; instead, sunlight strikes its gray, rocky surface, which reflects a modest fraction of that radiation back toward Earth, so the lunar radiance we admire is essentially borrowed sunshine.

At every moment, the Sun illuminates precisely one hemisphere of the Moon, namely the half oriented toward the Sun, while the opposite hemisphere remains in complete darkness.

The Moon travels around Earth along a path called its orbit, completing one entire cycle of appearances in approximately 29 and a half days, an interval that corresponds roughly to a calendar month.

As the Moon progresses along its orbit, observers on Earth perceive continuously varying proportions of its illuminated hemisphere, and astronomers designate each of these characteristic appearances as a phase.

At the new Moon, the sunlit hemisphere faces away from us, rendering the Moon practically invisible against the daytime sky. Shortly afterward, a slender crescent emerges, and the illuminated portion continues expanding, a stage astronomers characterize as waxing, until a half Moon and ultimately a full Moon become visible. Subsequently, the illuminated portion diminishes, a process designated as waning, until the cycle recommences. The intermediate phases immediately preceding and following the full Moon, when more than half the lunar disk is illuminated, are described as gibbous.

A widespread misconception maintains that the darkened portion represents Earth's shadow, but this explanation is fundamentally incorrect, since it is simply the side of the Moon oriented away from the Sun.

Furthermore, because the Moon requires precisely as long to rotate once on its axis as it does to complete an orbit of Earth, it perpetually keeps the identical side turned toward us.

In Saudi Arabia, each month of the Hijri calendar officially commences when the new crescent is sighted after sunset.

Because a complete cycle lasts approximately 29 and a half days, every Hijri month contains either 29 or 30 days, and the Hijri year is consequently about eleven days shorter than the solar year.

Consequently, you can demonstrate these phases yourself using an ordinary lamp and a ball: darken a room, switch on the lamp, hold the ball at arm's length, and rotate slowly in a circle, observing that as you turn, the illuminated region of the ball expands from a crescent to a complete circle and subsequently contracts again, precisely mirroring the behavior of the genuine Moon. In this demonstration, the lamp represents the Sun, the ball represents the Moon, and your head represents Earth.

versions.title: The Phases of the Moon
versions.text:
The Moon generates no light of its own; every glow it casts into the night sky is reflected sunlight. At any given moment, the Sun illuminates exactly one hemisphere of the Moon, just as it illuminates exactly one hemisphere of Earth, yet because the Moon continuously orbits our planet, the proportion of its illuminated hemisphere that remains visible from Earth changes night after night, thereby producing the familiar cycle of lunar phases. This orbital journey requires approximately twenty-nine and a half days to complete, a period that governs the rhythm of the entire phase cycle.

The sequence commences at the new moon, when the Moon's illuminated hemisphere faces entirely away from Earth, leaving the visible side shrouded in darkness. From there, a waxing crescent gradually materializes, expanding into a half moon, then becoming a waxing gibbous, before culminating in the full moon, when the Moon's entire visible face becomes illuminated. The cycle then reverses: a waning gibbous progressively shrinks to a half moon, then diminishes further into a waning crescent, before eventually returning once more to new moon, whereupon the pattern begins anew.

A common misconception holds that the darkened portion of the Moon during its various phases results directly from Earth's shadow falling across its surface. This assumption is fundamentally incorrect; Earth's shadow instead causes lunar eclipses, a distinct and considerably less frequent astronomical phenomenon. The darkness observed during ordinary phases simply reflects which particular part of the Moon's surface happens to be facing the Sun at that specific moment, rather than any obstruction caused by Earth itself.

Another subtlety concerns the Moon's rotational behavior. The Moon does, in fact, rotate steadily on its own axis, but its rotational period matches its orbital period with such precision that the same lunar hemisphere always faces Earth, meaning observers on our planet never glimpse the Moon's far side without the aid of specialized spacecraft.

This cycle additionally carries significant cultural and religious importance. Hijri calendar months begin with the sighting of the new crescent moon, and because the lunar cycle does not divide evenly into whole days, each month lasts either twenty-nine or thirty days. A simple demonstration employing a lamp to represent the Sun, a small ball to represent the Moon, and one's own head to represent Earth can vividly illustrate why these phases occur precisely as they do.

Understanding this cycle possesses considerable practical value extending well beyond astronomy alone, since knowing which particular phase the Moon currently occupies allows observers to accurately predict how much natural illumination will remain available after sunset on any given night of the month.

Astronomers and ordinary observers alike have relied upon this remarkably predictable rhythm for thousands of years, long before any formal written calendar existed to record it systematically.

versions.title: The Phases of the Moon
versions.text:
The Moon generates no illumination of its own; every trace of light it casts across the night sky is, in fact, sunlight reflected from its surface. At any given instant, the Sun illuminates precisely one hemisphere of the Moon, just as it simultaneously illuminates precisely one hemisphere of Earth, yet because the Moon continuously progresses along its orbital path around our planet, the particular portion of its illuminated hemisphere visible from Earth shifts incrementally from night to night, generating the recognizable sequence of lunar phases. This orbital journey requires approximately twenty-nine and a half days to complete, a duration that governs the rhythm of the entire phase cycle from beginning to end.

The sequence commences at new moon, a configuration in which the Moon's illuminated hemisphere faces entirely away from Earth, rendering the visible face dark. Thereafter, a waxing crescent gradually emerges, expanding progressively into a half moon, then a waxing gibbous, before culminating in the full moon, at which point the Moon's entire visible face appears illuminated. The cycle subsequently reverses direction: a waning gibbous diminishes into a half moon, then into a waning crescent, before ultimately returning once again to new moon, whereupon the entire pattern recommences.

A persistent misconception holds that the darkened portion of the Moon observable during its various phases results from Earth's shadow being cast across its surface. This belief is mistaken; Earth's shadow is instead responsible for lunar eclipses, a distinct and considerably less frequent astronomical phenomenon. The darkness observed during ordinary phases reflects nothing more than which particular region of the Moon's surface happens, at that moment, to face the Sun directly, rather than any obstruction imposed by Earth's intervening bulk.

A further subtlety concerns the Moon's own rotation. The Moon does indeed rotate about its axis, yet its rotational period corresponds so precisely with its orbital period that the identical lunar hemisphere perpetually faces Earth, meaning that observers situated on our planet never glimpse the Moon's far side unaided by spacecraft specifically dispatched for that purpose.

This recurring cycle additionally carries considerable cultural and religious significance. Hijri calendar months are traditionally reckoned to begin with the sighting of the new crescent moon, and because the lunar cycle does not divide evenly into whole days, each resulting month spans either twenty-nine or thirty days depending on observational timing. A straightforward demonstration employing a lamp to represent the Sun, a ball to represent the Moon, and one's own head to represent Earth can vividly and convincingly illustrate precisely why these phases unfold in the sequence and manner that they do, offering an intuitive grasp of an otherwise abstract astronomical mechanism.

Understanding this recurring cycle carries considerable practical value extending well beyond pure astronomical curiosity alone, since knowing precisely which phase the Moon currently occupies allows observers to predict with reasonable confidence how much natural illumination will be available after sunset on any particular night throughout the month, information that proved essential to travelers and farmers alike long before electric lighting became commonplace.

wrong.C: The side facing away from the Sun is dark.
wrong.D: Even at the new Moon, half is lit; it just faces away from us.

questions.stem: About how long does one full cycle of Moon phases take?
options: About 7 days, or one week
12 hours
29 and a half days
365 days, or one whole year
questions.why: The article says the Moon completes one cycle of shapes in about 29 and a half days.

wrong.A: About a week takes the Moon from crescent to full, not a whole cycle.
wrong.B: That is about half a day, far too short.
wrong.D: That is the length of a year.

questions.stem: The article says that when the bright part keeps growing, it is called waxing. What does waxing mean?
options: Turning dark
Becoming shiny
Moving away from Earth
Getting bigger
questions.why: The sentence says the bright part keeps growing, and that is what waxing means.

wrong.A: Turning dark is closer to waning.
wrong.B: The word is about size, not shine.
wrong.C: The Moon does not move away from Earth here.

questions.stem: Why is the Moon almost invisible at the new Moon?
options: Clouds always cover it then.
Its sunlit side faces away from us.
It stops reflecting light.
Earth's shadow hides it.
questions.why: At the new Moon, the lit side faces away from Earth, so we see almost nothing.

wrong.A: The article does not mention clouds.
wrong.C: It still reflects sunlight, just not toward us.
wrong.D: The article says the dark part is not Earth's shadow.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the paragraph about the new Moon, crescent, half Moon, and full Moon?
options: As a problem and a solution
As a list of opinions
In time order, as a cycle
As a comparison of two planets
questions.why: The paragraph uses words like next, until, and after that to show the phases in order.

wrong.B: The paragraph gives facts, not opinions.
wrong.D: Only the Moon and Earth are discussed, and not as a comparison.

questions.stem: One night the Moon is more than half lit, and the next night the lit part is a little smaller. Which phase is it?
options: A waning gibbous Moon
A waxing crescent
A new Moon
A waxing gibbous Moon
questions.why: More than half lit means gibbous, and shrinking means waning.

wrong.B: A crescent is less than half lit, and waxing means growing.
wrong.C: At the new Moon we see almost nothing.
wrong.D: Waxing would mean the lit part is growing, not shrinking.

questions.stem: What can you infer from the fact that the Moon always shows us the same side?
options: The Moon does not move at all.
People on Earth never see some parts of the Moon.
The Moon has no dark side.
The far side is Earth's shadow.
questions.why: If the same side always faces us, the other side is never seen from Earth.

wrong.A: The Moon moves along its orbit.
wrong.C: Half of the Moon is always dark.
wrong.D: The article says the dark part is not Earth's shadow.

MID.prompt: Describe the Moon's cycle from one new Moon to the next. Use the words waxing, waning, and gibbous.
checklist: I put the phases in the correct order.
I used waxing, waning, and gibbous correctly.
I explained that the Sun always lights half of the Moon.
MID.modelAnswer: The Sun always lights exactly half of the Moon, and the cycle starts at the new Moon, when that lit half faces away from us so the Moon looks almost invisible. The bright part keeps growing, which is called waxing, through a crescent, a half Moon, a gibbous phase, and finally a full Moon. After that, the bright part shrinks, which is called waning, moving back through gibbous and crescent shapes until the cycle begins again at the next new Moon.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The Moon slowly shrinks and grows in size each month.
Earth's shadow causes the Moon's changing shape.
The Hijri calendar was invented to measure the Moon.
We see changing parts of the Moon's sunlit half.
questions.why: The article explains that the Moon itself does not change; our view of its lit hemisphere does as it orbits.

wrong.A: The article says the Moon itself never changes.
wrong.B: The article calls this a misconception.
wrong.C: The calendar is one detail, not the central idea.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is the source of the Moon's glow?
options: Hot rock inside the Moon
Sunlight reflected by its surface
Light given off by Earth's cities
Gas burning on its surface
questions.why: The article says the lunar glow is "borrowed sunshine" reflected by its rocky surface.

wrong.A: The article says the Moon generates no light.
wrong.D: Nothing burns on the Moon in the article.

questions.stem: Why does the Moon always keep the same side turned toward Earth?
options: It takes as long to rotate once as to orbit Earth.
It does not rotate at all as it moves around Earth.
Earth's shadow holds it in place.
The Sun lights only that side.
questions.why: The article explains that one rotation takes as long as one orbit, so the same side faces us.

wrong.B: The article says the Moon does rotate.
wrong.C: Earth's shadow is not the reason.
wrong.D: The Sun lights different sides as the Moon moves.

questions.stem: The author writes that the lunar glow is "essentially borrowed sunshine." What does this phrase suggest?
options: The Moon will give the light back later.
The Moon steals light from the stars.
The light we see from the Moon really belongs to the Sun.
Sunshine is weaker on the Moon.
questions.why: "Borrowed" shows that the Moon's light is not its own; it comes from the Sun.

wrong.A: The phrase is a comparison, not a promise to return anything.
wrong.B: Stars are not mentioned as a source.
wrong.D: The phrase is about where the light comes from, not its strength.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the lamp-and-ball model at the end?
options: To prove that the Moon is the same size as a ball
To let readers test the explanation for themselves
To explain how lamps produce light
To show that the phases happen inside houses
questions.why: The model lets readers see with their own eyes how a lit ball shows phases as it moves.

wrong.A: The model is about light and position, not size.
wrong.C: The article does not explain how lamps work.
wrong.D: The real phases happen in space; the model only copies them.

questions.stem: Which phase comes directly between the half Moon after the new Moon and the full Moon?
options: Waning crescent
New Moon
Waning gibbous
Waxing gibbous
questions.why: After the half Moon, the lit part keeps growing (waxing) and is more than half lit (gibbous) before the full Moon.

wrong.A: Waning phases come after the full Moon.
wrong.B: The new Moon starts the cycle.
wrong.C: Waning gibbous comes after the full Moon.

questions.stem: At a full Moon, where is Earth most likely to be?
options: Between the Sun and the Moon
Behind the Sun
On the far side of the Moon from the Sun
Exactly where the Moon is
questions.why: At the new Moon the lit side faces away from us, so at the full Moon, halfway around, we face the lit side, with Earth between the Sun and the Moon.

wrong.B: Earth cannot see the lit side from behind the Sun.
wrong.C: Then the Moon would be between Earth and the Sun, which is the new Moon.
wrong.D: Earth and the Moon cannot be in the same place.

questions.stem: Why are some Hijri months 29 days long and others 30 days long?
options: Because the Sun moves faster in some months
Because the Moon's cycle lasts about 29 and a half days
Because Earth's shadow covers the crescent
Because every month has one full Moon and two new Moons
questions.why: A cycle that lasts about 29 and a half days cannot fit into whole months of the same length, so months must be 29 or 30 days.

wrong.A: The article does not say the Sun changes speed.
wrong.C: The article calls the shadow idea a misconception.
wrong.D: A cycle has one new Moon and one full Moon.

HIGH.prompt: A friend says the Moon's dark part is Earth's shadow. Write a paragraph explaining why this is a misconception and what really causes the phases.
checklist: I explained that the Sun always lights one hemisphere of the Moon.
I explained how the Moon's orbit changes what we see.
I used at least two key words correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: My friend's idea that the Moon's dark part is Earth's shadow is a common misconception, but the article makes clear that the Sun always illuminates exactly one hemisphere of the Moon, the half that faces the Sun, while the opposite hemisphere simply stays in darkness because sunlight never reaches it. The real cause of the lunar phases is the Moon's orbit around Earth: as it travels along that path, we on Earth see different portions of its lit half, from a thin crescent to a full Moon and back again, which has nothing to do with Earth blocking sunlight.
